html:
A Mesoamerican way of counting days from a fixed starting point, which falls in August 3114 BCE in our calendar. The oldest known Long Count dates were carved in the 1st century BCE, at Chiapa de Corzo in Chiapas and at Tres Zapotes on the Gulf Coast, where Stela C gives a date of 32 BCE.

The count mostly works in twenties:

  • 1 kin is a day; 20 kins make a winal.
  • 18 winals make a tun of 360 days.
  • 20 tuns make a katun; 20 katuns make a baktun of about 394 years.

To write a number like this you need a sign for an empty place, so the Long Count is one of the earliest uses of zero as a placeholder, centuries before the Indian zero of the Gwalior inscription.

The Maya used it on their monuments, written in Maya script, until about 900 CE. The end of the 13th baktun, on 21 December 2012, set off a wave of doomsday stories that the Maya themselves never told.
